newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Russia supply worry fuels nickel rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia supply worry fuels nickel rally.

text.p: The price of nickel rose briskly on Monday on fears about Russian supply because of labour unrest at the giant Norilsk metals complex in the Arctic.
Nickel, mainly used in making stainless steel, had been consolidating in a broad uptrend in recent weeks.
It blasted above the key $8,000 per tonne threshold on the London Metal Exchange on news that disgruntled workers at Norilsk may discuss disrupting output over wage delays.
The day's high at $8,110 was up $235 from Friday and the strongest since May 1996.
Three months delivery LME aluminium also bustled higher on technical buying to finish the afternoon at $1,654 per tonne, a gain of $23 from Friday.
"It's all technical with aluminium right now," an LME floor trader said, adding that trade selling was coming in above the market to keep a check on the rise.
Copper made a new 8-1/2 month high at $2,385 per tonne before profit-taking took the top off the rally and it eased to stand little changed on the day.
The industrial metals have all rallied this year. But in their latest Commodities Outlook, researchers at UBS Ltd say prospects for global economic expansion are a wild card.
"Visions of increasing base metal output cloud price prospects but similar hallucinations failed to materialise last year," their report says.
They reckon that aluminium demand should exceed even a 3.0 percent growth in supply in 1997 but copper demand may lag behind the expansion of availability.
Gold was seen trying to consolidate on Monday in a new range between $350 and $355 an ounce after a dramatic fund-led rally last week.
Bullion had soared almost $10 in a day at the end of last week, close to $355, rebounding from recent 3-3/4 year lows.
Monday saw an afternoon fix of $353.05 in more subdued activity. Physical demand for gold was strong in Asia.
Bellwether North Sea Brent Crude Oil futures are around their lowest in six months - below $20 a barrel, compared with around $25 late last year.
The slide has reflected an ample supply of crude now that the United Nations has eased its Gulf War embargo against Iraq and the arrival of warmer weather on both sides of the Atlantic.
London May Brent futures traded below $19.50 on Monday.

Chicago grains futures were firm after speculative funds took an interest on Friday, particularly in corn (maize) which, at Friday's close of $2.91-3/4 for March. was at its highest since October 15. It held close to that on Monday morning.
Funds on Friday bought some 40-50 million bushels of corn, bringing estimated purchases for the week above 300 million.
"These guys are relentless," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co. "Every day they're buying."
Wheat also benefited from the speculative frenzy, with March closing Friday up 9-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.73. Monday saw it still around those levels by the midsession.

Traders said world wheat supplies looked in much better shape this year than last, although worries about spring wheat planting delays due to heavy snows in the northern Midwest and low winter wheat plantings last autumn were supportive.
The new UBS Ltd forecast for commodities saw the wheat market as volatile because stocks are low.
Elsewhere, UBS sees a general unease in the coffee market because fundamentals do not explain current strength.
Coffee futures rallied this year by almost 50 percent in the first six weeks of the year but speculator selling has taken some of the froth off the market in recent days.
London robusta coffee futures extended a decline to trade around $1,530 per tonne compared with $1,705 on February 14.
"Development of coffee prices will primarily depend on this year's harvest in Brazil - here crop estimates still vary substantially," says the UBS report .
